opus-5.5.text:
I think the core reason is that post-training and pre-training are really two very different kinds of work, both in their goals and in the skills and infrastructure they need.

Pre-training is, in a sense, a fairly well-defined engineering problem. You have a huge amount of data, a clear objective, next-token prediction, and the main questions are about scale: how to clean the data, how to make the cluster run stably, how to push compute efficiency. It's like building a very big, very solid foundation. The feedback loop is long. You train for months and then you see what you got.

Post-training is different. What you're doing there is shaping behavior. You're asking: what do we actually want this model to do? Should it reason step by step, use tools, write code, act as an agent, refuse certain things, have a certain personality? Those are product and research questions at the same time, and they change very quickly. The iteration cycle is much shorter. You might run dozens of experiments a week, look at the outputs, find some strange behavior, fix the reward, fix the data, and run again.

Especially now with reinforcement learning becoming central, post-training has its own very specific technical stack. RL systems look nothing like pre-training systems. You have generation, which is inference-heavy, and training interleaved together. You have reward models or verifiers, environments, sandboxes for code execution, long-horizon agent rollouts. The bottlenecks are different. In pre-training, GPU utilization is relatively easy to keep high. In RL, you have long-tail rollouts and asynchronous scheduling problems, which is why we spent a lot of effort building asynchronous RL systems. If you just ask the pre-training team to also do this, they're optimizing for a totally different kind of workload.

There's also a people aspect. Good post-training people need a kind of taste. They need to look at model outputs and quickly sense what's wrong, whether it's reward hacking, whether the model is being lazy, whether the data distribution is off. That intuition is pretty different from what makes someone a great pre-training engineer. And because post-training is close to the final user experience, the team needs to talk constantly with the product side and with evaluation.

So I'd say it's not that the two are unrelated. Actually they need to collaborate very closely, because what the base model has learned determines the ceiling of what post-training can elicit. But the rhythm, the methodology and the infrastructure are different enough that if you don't give post-training its own team, it tends to get treated as a small finishing step at the end, and today that's simply not true anymore. A lot of the capability you see in reasoning models and agents actually comes out of post-training.

r001.rationale: The response gives differences in goals, infrastructure, iteration, and expertise as reasons for a separate team, but does not mention researchers’ access to actual user data.

r002.rationale: It says post-training elicits capability from the base model, but does not state that actual user data alone is insufficient to bring out the model’s highest intelligence.

r003.rationale: The response does not propose feeding actual user data back into pre-training.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd say the simplest answer is that post-training is a fundamentally different kind of problem from pre-training, even though they share the same model and the same infrastructure.

Pre-training is, in a sense, a very clean problem. You have a huge corpus, you have a loss function, and the main questions are about data quality, scale, and systems efficiency. The signal is dense and the objective is well-defined. Once the pipeline is running, a lot of the work is about making it run bigger and faster.

Post-training is messy. You're no longer asking "did the model predict the next token well," you're asking "does the model behave the way a person wants it to behave." That involves human preferences, reward models, reinforcement learning, and a lot of judgment about what "good" even means. The objective itself is something you have to design, and it keeps changing as you learn more about how users actually interact with the model.

That difference shows up in the skills you need. Post-training needs people who deeply understand RL, because the algorithms are finicky and unstable in ways supervised learning is not. It needs people who think carefully about evaluation, because if your evals are wrong, RL will happily optimize the wrong thing. And it needs people with taste about data, who can look at a batch of human annotations and tell whether they're actually teaching the model something useful. Those are not the same people who are best at squeezing another few percent of MFU out of a cluster.

The iteration loop is also different. Pre-training runs are long and expensive, so you do a lot of careful planning up front. Post-training is about running many experiments quickly, looking at outputs, finding failure modes, adjusting the reward or the data, and running again. The culture that works well for that is closer to a fast product team than to a large-scale systems team.

And honestly, there's a resourcing argument too. If post-training is just a side task of the pre-training team, it will always be the thing that gets squeezed when the big run needs attention. Having a separate team with its own roadmap means someone is actually accountable for how the model behaves at the end, not just how it scores on perplexity.

So I don't think of it as splitting one job in two. I think of it as recognizing that there were two jobs all along.

r001.rationale: The response discusses post-training expertise and team accountability, but does not identify capability researchers’ lack of access to actual user data as a reason for a separate team.

r002.rationale: It does not state that actual user data alone is insufficient to bring out a model’s highest intelligence.

r003.rationale: It does not propose feeding actual user data back into pre-training.

astra-6.text:
I think post-training needs a separate team because the objective and the way you work are quite different from pre-training. In pre-training, you’re largely focused on building a strong foundation: the data, the architecture, and how efficiently you can scale training. In post-training, the question becomes: how do you turn that capability into behavior that people actually find useful?

That requires a much tighter loop between training and evaluation. You try something, look at the model’s responses, figure out whether the problem comes from the data, the reward signal, or the evaluation itself, and iterate. A model can improve on a benchmark while becoming less helpful in real conversations, so you need people who own that whole loop.

A dedicated team gives that work a clear focus and accountability. But separate shouldn’t mean isolated. The post-training team still needs to work closely with pre-training and product, because what you can achieve depends on both the underlying model and what users need from it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think post-training has a different feedback loop from pre-training. In pre-training, you’re largely focused on improving the model’s general capabilities through data, architecture, and scale. In post-training, the question becomes: how do you turn those capabilities into behavior that’s useful to people? That involves instruction following, reasoning, tool use, and learning from feedback.

You need a team that can iterate closely with the people using the model, figure out where it fails, and turn those failures into better training data and evaluations. That’s a different rhythm and requires a somewhat different mix of skills. But a separate team shouldn’t mean an isolated team—the findings from post-training should also inform the next round of pre-training.
